chapter_theme: In the Katturai Kaathai the goddess of Madurai, the Pandya's family deity, pleads the justice of his line with legends of Pandya self-punishment and repair, then gives Kannaki the cause from a former birth, Kovalan's killing of Sangaman and the widow Neeli's curse, and the pathini goes up from Murugan's hill to heaven with her husband.

cast.role: the guardian goddess of Madurai, family deity of the Pandyas, who tells Kannaki the cause from a former birth (calls herself மதுரா பதி)
Kovalan's wife, the pathini who burned Madurai
merchant of Puhar, Kannaki's husband, killed in Madurai
the Pandya king of Madurai who had Kovalan killed (here the goddess's கோமகன்)
the wife of the poor brahmin Keeranthai, left in the king's protection
a Pandya of old, of the hand that broke Indra's crown, whose sceptre cut off his own hand (not named in the Tamil)
a learned brahmin of the Chola land who won gifts from the Chera
Vaarthikan's small son, named after the god under the banyan, who recites the Veda before Parasaran
a brahmin of Thangal, imprisoned on the charge of taking treasure
the Pandya's officers who seize Vaarthikan
the Pandya of old who freed Vaarthikan and made amends (not named in the Tamil)
the goddess Kotravai, whose temple door stays shut (also கலையமர் செல்வி, கொற்றவை)
a merchant of Singapuram in Kalinga, killed as a spy in a former age
Kovalan in his former birth, a king's officer who had Sangaman killed
king of Singapuram in Kalinga, at enmity with his kinsman Kumaran
Sangaman's wife, who laid the curse
the retinue of the king of the gods who take Kannaki to heaven

silappathikaram:23:1-17.reading: The narrator describes the goddess of Madurai, half dark and half golden, a lotus in her left hand and a sword in her right, a warrior's anklet on one foot and a woman's anklet on the other, who, as the family goddess of the Pandya, does not come before the grieving pathini but appears behind her and asks her to hear her plea.
silappathikaram:23:1-17.nuance: The goddess's two halves, the woman's anklet (சிலம்பு) on one foot and the hero's anklet (கழல்) on the other, set the book's emblem on a divided body. She stands behind Kannaki (பின்னிலைத் தோன்றி) because she is the Pandya's own family goddess (குலமுதற் கிழத்தி ஆதலின்), and the word she uses is குறை, a petition: the city's deity comes as a pleader for the king.
silappathikaram:23:1-17.event: The goddess of Madurai appears behind Kannaki and asks her to hear her plea.

silappathikaram:23:18-32.reading: Kannaki turns and asks who follows her and whether she knows her grief; the goddess answers that she knows it, names herself the deity of Madurai, grieved for what befell Kannaki's husband, asks her to hear what came to her king when his former deed arrived and what came to her husband, and says the Pandya kings' ears heard only the sound of the Veda, never the sound of the justice bell.
silappathikaram:23:18-32.nuance: The goddess gives the one cause to both men: ஊழ்வினை came to her king (line 28) and the deed came to harm Kannaki's husband (line 30), so the king is not the only one whose fault is being judged. Lines 25 to 30 are three short couplet-like pairs set inside the akaval. Her boast that the bell was never rung answers Kannaki's plea before the Pandya, where the Chola's gate bell trembled for the cow.
silappathikaram:23:18-32.event: Kannaki asks who follows her, and the goddess names herself and asks to be heard.

claims.claim: the king's fall came because his former deed arrived
a just king's line never needed the bell rung by those wronged

silappathikaram:23:33-44.reading: The goddess says the Pandya's sceptre brings blame on his people only when they are kings who will not bow to him, that in this noble line joined to good conduct even untamed youth, an elephant in must not yet held by the goad of learning, brings no fault, and begins the tale of the wife of the poor brahmin Keeranthai, at whose door someone knocked one night.
silappathikaram:23:33-44.nuance: The claim that the line's youth stays blameless without learning is made by the line's own goddess, in the chapter that tells how its present king failed. The masculine புடைத்தனன் (line 43) leaves who knocked to the next lines, where the king's response shows it was he.
silappathikaram:23:33-44.event: One night a man knocks at the door of Keeranthai's wife, whose husband is away.

claims.claim: the Pandya's sceptre harms none of its people, only kings who refuse to bow
those born in a noble line joined to good conduct do not fall into fault even in untamed youth

silappathikaram:23:45-69.reading: Keeranthai's wife cries that her husband left her saying there is no fence but the king's, and asks whether that fence does not guard her today; the king, his heart burned as if a hot nail were driven into his ear, cuts off his own hand, the hand that broke Indra's crown, and the goddess turns to a second tale, of the brahmin Parasaran of the Chola land, who set out to see the Chera famed for his gifts and came among the brahmins of the three fires and four Vedas.
silappathikaram:23:45-69.nuance: The king punishes his own hand for a wrong of approach that the wife only feared, so the goddess sets a Pandya against the Chola exemplars Kannaki had thrown at him; she even names the Chola of the dove and the calf (line 58) here, as the ruler of Parasaran's land, and the burning heart (நெஞ்சஞ் சுடுதலின்) is the phrase Kannaki used of the Chola who killed his son.
silappathikaram:23:45-69.event: Hearing the woman's reproach, the Pandya cuts off his own hand; Parasaran sets out for the Chera court.

claims.claim: the king's protection is the only fence a woman left alone needs
a king of the true line punishes his own body for a fault against his subjects

silappathikaram:23:70-85.reading: Parasaran wins the brahmins' victory garland in debate, receives fine jewels and, going home, rests at Thangal, a brahmins' town of the Pandya, under the pipal of its common hall, setting down his staff, water pot, umbrella and bundle, and hails the Chera who cut the kadamba in the sea and carved his bow on the hill, the Poraiyan of the Porunai, Mantharam Cheral.
silappathikaram:23:70-85.nuance: A Chola-land brahmin, standing in a Pandya village, sings the Chera's praise; the four வாழி lines join epithets the Sangam books give to different Cheras, and the Tamil does not say whether they name one king or several.
silappathikaram:23:70-85.event: Parasaran, enriched by the Chera, rests at Thangal and blesses the Chera king.

silappathikaram:23:86-102.reading: Parasaran calls the playing children to recite with him for his bundle, and Vaarthikan's small son, named after the god under the banyan, recites the Veda without fault though his tongue still lisps; Parasaran, delighted, gives Thakkinan a pearl thread, bangles and earrings and goes home, and the king's officers, unable to bear the boy wearing them, seize Vaarthikan as a brahmin who took treasure without the king's leave.
silappathikaram:23:86-102.nuance: The charge (கோமுறை அன்றிப் படுபொருள் வௌவிய) is the officers' own; the text gives envy as their motive (பொறாஅராகி), not any order of the king.
silappathikaram:23:86-102.event: Parasaran rewards the boy who recites the Veda, and the king's officers seize the boy's father as a thief.

silappathikaram:23:103-122.reading: Vaarthikan is put in prison; his wife Kaarthigai weeps and rolls on the ground, the door of Aiyai's temple will not open, and the king, asking whether his sceptre has bent, learns the truth, declares that his rule has strayed through ignorant men and asks the people to bear his fault, gives Thangal and Vayalur to Vaarthikan, and lies prostrate on the earth to soothe Kaarthigai's grief.
silappathikaram:23:103-122.nuance: The king reads a shut temple door as the sign of a bent sceptre (கொடுங்கோ லுண்டுகொல், line 111) and owns the wrong of his servants as his own (என் இறைமுறை பிழைத்தது). Lines 121 to 122 (திருமார்பு நல்கியவள் ... தணித்தனனே) may mean that he lay with his chest to the earth before her, or something else; the word division is unclear.
silappathikaram:23:103-122.event: When Aiyai's temple door stays shut, the king learns of the wrongful arrest, frees Vaarthikan and grants him villages.

claims.claim: when a god's door stays shut the king's justice has failed
a king answers for the wrongs his servants do in his name

silappathikaram:23:123-137.reading: The goddess's door opens, the king has it proclaimed by drum on an elephant's neck that the prisons be broken and the guilty set free and that treasure found or laid by belong to those who hold it, and the goddess tells Kannaki to hear how a king of this line that proclaimed justice came to err, for there is also a saying that on the eighth day of the dark half of Aadi, under Krittika, on a Friday, fire will eat Madurai and its king will perish.
silappathikaram:23:123-137.nuance: Line 131 to 132 may set the proclaiming king against the present one, or say that the same line which proclaimed justice now erred; either way the goddess adds a fixed omen-day (lines 133 to 136) to the deed of a former birth, so the burning is foretold as well as earned.
silappathikaram:23:123-137.event: The temple door opens and the king proclaims the release of prisoners; the goddess cites a prophecy of Madurai's burning.

claims.claim: the burning of Madurai and the fall of its king were foretold to a fixed day

silappathikaram:23:138-160.reading: The goddess tells how in Kalinga two kings of one line, Vasu of Singapuram and Kumaran of Kapilapuram, were at war so that none could cross the land between, how the merchant Sangaman came secretly with his wife to sell jewels in the market, and how Kannaki's husband in his former birth, Bharatan, an officer of the king who had left his vow, seized him as a spy and had him killed, so that his widow Neeli cried whether this was the justice of kings or of the Bharatas.
silappathikaram:23:138-160.nuance: This is the former deed the patikam only names: Kovalan once played the part the goldsmith plays now, bringing a stranger with goods before a king as a criminal and having him killed. The text gives Bharatan's motive as a dislike that came from having left his vow (விரத நீங்கிய வெறுப்பினன்), so his own fault, not only fate, is named.
silappathikaram:23:138-160.event: In a former birth Bharatan seizes the merchant Sangaman as a spy and has him killed.

silappathikaram:23:161-176.reading: Neeli cried through the halls and streets, and after fourteen days climbed a hill to join her slain husband in the sky and, falling, laid the curse that those who caused her sorrow should suffer the same; the goddess tells Kannaki that she and her husband are under that curse, that when the deed of a former birth rises penance does not help those not upright, and that she will see her husband within fourteen days, but only in a god's form.
silappathikaram:23:161-176.nuance: Neeli's curse is for exact repetition (எம்முறு துயரம் ... தம்முறு துயரம்), and the story repays it in kind: a wife again cries through a city's streets after her husband's killing. செம்மையிலோர் (line 172) is not named; it may be Bharatan's past, or a general rule.
silappathikaram:23:161-176.event: Neeli curses the killers as she falls from a hill; the goddess tells Kannaki she will see Kovalan in fourteen days in divine form.

claims.claim: a curse laid in grief by one wronged makes the wrongdoers suffer the same sorrow
when a former deed rises in wrath, penance does not help those who are not upright

silappathikaram:23:177-200.reading: After the goddess has told the pathini the course of fate and the fire has withdrawn, Kannaki vows neither to sit nor stand until she sees her husband, breaks her bangles at Kotravai's gate, says she came in by the east gate with her husband and goes out by the west alone, follows the Vaigai's bank night and day, climbs Murugan's hill and under a flowering vengai mourns that she is a woman of fiery deeds, and after fourteen days the retinue of the king of the gods praises her, rains flowers and takes her up in the sky car with Kovalan.
silappathikaram:23:177-200.nuance: Kannaki now calls herself தீத்தொழிலாட்டி, a doer of the deed of fire, where at the burning she declared herself faultless; Kovalan is still கோநகர் பிழைத்த, he who erred against (or perished in) the royal city, even as he is taken to heaven.
silappathikaram:23:177-200.event: Kannaki leaves Madurai by the west gate, climbs the hill and after fourteen days is taken to heaven with Kovalan.

silappathikaram:23:201-204.reading: A closing venba says it is certain that the gods worship the woman who worships her husband rather than a god, for Kannaki, ornament of the women of earth, has become the guest of the women of heaven.
silappathikaram:23:201-204.nuance: The first line takes up three words of Kural 55's first line (தெய்வந் தொழாஅள் கொழுநற்), short of the four-word echo rule, and changes the reward: not rain at the wife's command but the gods' own worship of her.

claims.claim: the gods worship the wife who worships her husband rather than a god

links.note: The Alarpadu Kaathai ends with the goddess of Madurai appearing before (முன்) the pathini, unable to bear the fire; here she will not stand before her and appears behind her, being the Pandya's family goddess.
links.teaches: Read together, the goddess's first coming is driven by the fire, but her place behind Kannaki shows that the city's deity arrives as an embarrassed advocate of the guilty king's house.

links.note: Kannaki shamed the Pandya with the Chola whose gate bell's tongue trembled for the cow; the goddess replies that the Pandya kings' ears heard the Veda's tongue (மறைநா) and never the bell's tongue (மணிநா).
links.teaches: The goddess turns Kannaki's proof of the Chola's justice into evidence for the Pandya: a line whose bell no one ever had to ring needed no such exemplar, so the dispute over the king's justice becomes a dispute between two dynasties' records.

links.note: The patikam's third moral is that the former deed comes in wrath and makes one eat it; the goddess says ஊழ்வினை came to her king as well as to Kannaki's husband.
links.teaches: The patikam keeps karma for the story's sufferers and the death-dealing dharma for the king, but the goddess applies ஊழ்வினை to the king himself, so the first and third morals meet in one person.

links.note: The couplet says those born of good family do not slip (இழுக்கார்) in conduct; the goddess says those born in the Pandya line joined to conduct (ஒழுக்கொடு) suffer no fault (இழுக்கம்) even in untamed youth.
links.teaches: The couplet's rule about good birth is spoken by the dynasty's own goddess while she excuses its present king, so the epic shows the rule used as a family's defence at the moment its member has failed.

gains.a: the goddess's boast gains a recognised maxim behind it, which is why it carries weight against Kannaki's charge
gains.b: the couplet gains a test: the chapter itself tells of a king of that line who erred, so good birth does not guarantee what the couplet claims

links.note: Kannaki cited the Chola who killed his own son under the wheel when the cow's tears burned his heart (நெஞ்சுசுட); the goddess answers with a Pandya who cut off his own hand when a woman's reproach burned his heart (நெஞ்சஞ் சுடுதலின்).
links.teaches: The two speeches match self-punishment for self-punishment, son for hand, showing that the argument over Kovalan's death is being fought with rival royal legends of the same pattern.

links.note: Parasaran hails the Chera who cut the kadamba in the sea (கடற்கடம் பெறிந்த) and carved his bow on the hill; Patitruppattu 11 tells the felling of the guarded kadamba after reaching the sea by Imayavaramban Neduncheralathan, whom the Himalaya marks.
links.teaches: The epic keeps the Sangam Chera's signature deed as a blessing formula in a brahmin's mouth, and strings it with Mantharam Cheral and the Porunai's Poraiyan, so the separate Cheras of the decades become one praised house.

gains.a: the brahmin's blessing gains a real deed and a named king behind its epithet
gains.b: the decade's battle gains an afterlife as a stock title, cited in a Pandya village by a Chola-land brahmin as the Chera's fame

links.note: The officers seize Vaarthikan because his son wears jewels a stranger gave; the goldsmith tells the king that the stranger with the anklet is the thief of the palace anklet.
links.teaches: The goddess's precedent is the same case as Kovalan's, a man holding valuable jewels wrongly taken for a thief by the king's men, chosen so that the old king's remedy can be measured against the present king's haste.

links.note: The old Pandya asks whether his sceptre has bent, admits his rule strayed through ignorant men and makes amends; Nedunjeliyan, shown the gem, says he is the thief and dies.
links.teaches: Both kings confess the fault as their own, but the ancestor's confession comes before any death and repairs it with land, while Nedunjeliyan's comes after and can only be paid with his life: the difference is when the king inquires.

links.note: The goddess cites a saying that fire will eat Madurai and its king on a fixed day of Aadi; the fire god says he had a command long before (பண்டே) to burn the city on the day the pathini was wronged.
links.teaches: Two separate voices, the omen and the fire god's standing order, make the burning predetermined, so Kannaki's act is shown as the trigger of a sentence already fixed.

links.note: Bharatan seized a stranger merchant with goods as a spy, showed him to the king and had him killed; in this life Kovalan, a stranger with an anklet, is shown to the king as a thief and killed without inquiry.
links.teaches: The former deed is the present crime with the roles reversed, so Kovalan suffers exactly the false accusation he once made, and the goldsmith takes the place he once held.

links.note: Neeli cried through the halls and streets asking whether this was justice and cursed the killers to suffer her sorrow; Kannaki cries through Madurai asking whether there are women, wise men or a god in the city.
links.teaches: Neeli's curse asked for the same sorrow, and Kannaki's lament fulfils it in form as well as fact, a widow's public cry against an unjust killing repeated in a new birth.

links.note: The quatrain says sin cannot stand before austerity while merit lasts; the goddess says that when a former deed rises in wrath penance does not help those not upright.
links.teaches: Both limit what austerity can do, but the quatrain makes merit run out with time, while the goddess makes the bar moral: penance fails against a ripened deed for those who lack uprightness.

gains.a: the goddess's saying gains a measure: austerity does guard, but only on terms
gains.b: the quatrain's limit gains a second condition and a case, the ascetic-guarded couple who still meet the deed of a former birth

links.note: At the burning Kannaki declared to the gods that she was without fault (குற்றமிலேன் யான்); under the vengai she laments that she is a woman of fiery deeds (தீத்தொழி லாட்டியேன் யான்).
links.teaches: Kannaki's own judgment of the burning reverses once the goddess has shown her the former deed, so the epic lets its heroine see her vengeance as a deed with its own weight just before it raises her to heaven.

links.note: The couplet says the wife who worships her husband rather than a god can command the rain; the venba takes its words and says the gods themselves worship such a wife.
links.teaches: The epic reads Kural 55 through Kannaki's end: the wife's power over nature becomes a claim on the gods, who now worship her, and the reward follows the burning of a city rather than a gift of rain.

gains.a: the venba gains the authority of the couplet's own words for its praise of Kannaki
gains.b: the couplet gains a case that tests it: its pathini wields fire and destruction, not rain, yet is still praised in its words

new_concepts.gloss: the chaste wife whose steadfastness gives her word power over kings, cities and nature
new_concepts.label_source: the unit's own word (பத்தினி line 14, மாபத் தினி line 177)

new_concepts.gloss: a curse, a word spoken in grief or anger that binds its object and comes to fruit, even in a later birth

source_issues: Lineation: the edition's printed line numbers end at 200 against 204 lines as shown (the closing venba is unnumbered or counted apart).

Lines 25 to 30 are three short couplet-like pairs (each a long line and a short one) set inside the akaval block with no metre rubric; line 30 ends one pair and resumes the akaval mid-line (வினை; காதின்).
Line 121 (இருநில மடந்தைக்குத் திருமார்பு நல்கியவள்) has an unclear word division (நல்கி அவள் or நல்கிய அவள்), and lines 121 to 122 are hard to construe.
Line 160 to 161: Neeli's cry (அரசர் முறையோ ... சேரியீர் முறையோவென) runs across the unit boundary at 160/161; the boundary was left as cut because other chapters already link to these unit ids.
